episode.title: Cariboo Signals - Indigenous Lands & Innovation
episode.description:
Riley and Casey explore technology and society in rural communities. Today's focus: Indigenous Lands & Innovation.

THIS WEEK WE'RE ASKING: Is trust something you build, or something you inherit?

NEWS ROUNDUP: We break down Prescribed burn planned near Esler Road and Jobs, growth, workforce challenges of Cariboo’s mining sector discussed in Williams Lake, plus 14 more stories, and explore what these developments mean for communities like ours.

RURAL CONNECTIONS: Deep dive on Indigenous Lands & Innovation Topics include: AI, infrastructure, funding.

Hosts: Riley (Tech optimist with an engineering background) and Casey (Community-first skeptic of tech promises).

COMMUNITY SPOTLIGHT: Cariboo Friendship Society

research.block:
PRE-RESEARCHED INSIGHTS FOR THE DEEP DIVE

RESEARCH QUESTION: What is the current status of the Na-Cho Nyäk Dun $150M lawsuit over the Eagle gold mine, and what are the governments arguing?

Findings: The First Nation of Na-Cho Nyäk Dun filed the claim in Yukon Supreme Court on December 9, 2025, against the Yukon government and the Government of Canada. It alleges negligence in the 2024 Eagle Gold Mine heap leach failure and says the Yukon government authorized nearly every mining project proposed in its territory, which it argues breached treaty rights. The First Nation has also asked Canada's auditor general to investigate the territorial government's handling of the incident. The APTN report says the Yukon and federal governments are seeking dismissal of the suit. By April 2026, Yukon News was reporting the First Nation challenging the territory over a possible sale of the mothballed mine and its disaster response. CBC has reported that the mine's receiver has sued its contractor for negligence, and that a Singapore-based company has emerged as a suitor for the mine. The First Nation has said it is neutral on the sale but criticized the process.
Suggested angle: This is the story's clearest test of "innovation" versus accountability. Riley can argue that the lawsuit shows that treaty-based co-governance and modern final agreements give Indigenous nations real legal leverage over resource development. Casey can counter that the claim is still unproven, that governments are asking for dismissal, and that a $150M lawsuit is a slow remedy for a contamination event. The auditor-general request and the sale process show that the real fight is over who controls decisions about a mine after operations fail, not over technology alone.

RESEARCH QUESTION: Why is the Nenqayni Wellness Centre closing, and what does it signal about funding for Indigenous health services in the Cariboo?

Findings: The Nenqayni Wellness Centre Society, which has served First Nations and Inuit youth, families and communities for more than 44 years, announced in October that it would close permanently in December. It cited "funding constraints and the inability to sustain bed-based programming." Staff have fallen from close to 60 to 14. Williams Lake Tribune reporting from November 2025 says the Xatsull First Nation decided not to renew the lease on the society's facility, which the nation will take over in 2026. The society has moved to mobile and in-community outreach. The program was originally funded by the First Nations Health Authority under the National Native Alcohol and Abuse Program. The society's own listing confirms that it is no longer accepting residential applications.
Suggested angle: The closure shows the gap between a "land-based healing" model and the funding structures that pay for it. Riley can frame the shift to in-community outreach as an innovation that brings care closer to home. Casey can point out that the change was driven by funding constraints and a lost facility lease, not by choice, and that the people who needed beds now have fewer options. Both can agree that the question is whether outreach can replace residential care.

RESEARCH QUESTION: What is the federal 2 Billion Trees program's role in Indigenous-led wildfire restoration, and how does the Cariboo shrub project fit?

Findings: The 2 Billion Trees program is a federal initiative that aims to plant two billion trees over ten years on provincial and federal Crown lands, in cities, and on Indigenous and private land. Natural Resources Canada says it has an Indigenous funding stream that is well along toward its target. Its British Columbia projects include restoration of areas hit by the 2021 Lytton wildfire, with a goal of about 46 million trees. Other Indigenous-led wildfire projects under the program include a WWF-Canada project in Secwepemc territory that plants 900,000 seedlings over three years through Indigenous leadership, and Skeetchestn Natural Resources work in the same region. The WWF-backed Splatsin/Secwepemc-led reforestation program reports more than 1.1 million trees planted and more than 677 hectares restored. The Central Chilcotin Rehabilitation shrub project, which uses the same program, is a smaller, culturally focused project that targets access to shrubs in community spaces, not timber or carbon outcomes.
Suggested angle: This is a useful case for testing whether federal climate money reaches small, community-defined goals. Riley can argue that the program is a model for Indigenous-led ecological repair that treats culturally important plants as infrastructure. Casey can ask whether a program built around tree counts (the "two billion" target) can measure cultural access, and who decides on success when the metric is a shrub used in ceremony rather than a seedling count. Both can ask how long-term monitoring will be funded after the planting season ends.

ELECTION RESEARCH — 2026 B.C. provincial general election

Background for the roundup's election stories and any race the hosts mention. It is not the deep dive's subject.

**FINDINGS — Cariboo-Chilcotin**

On the ballot: Kathryn Askew (BC NDP), Lorne Doerkson (Conservative), Douglas Gook (BC Green).

- **Kathryn Askew (BC NDP).** 100 Mile Free Press (Oct. 1, 2026) reports she is a retired school teacher from Canim Lake and the NDP candidate. The BC NDP release names her as its Cariboo-Chilcotin candidate and says she has 32 years in education, including leadership roles with the BC Teachers' Federation and her local union (bcndp.ca, undated in the copy read). The same release says that in 2025 she was the NDP candidate for Mission—Matsqui—Abbotsford in the federal election. Brad Vis (Conservative) won that riding with 56.7% and Jeff Howe (Liberal) placed second with 36.6% (stephentaylor.ca, 2025 results). Askew's own vote share in that race is not established: the Fraser Valley Current results page I opened carried no figures, and a pre-nomination Mission City Record piece names a different NDP candidate for the riding, so the show has not confirmed her 2025 result. No controversy involving Askew was found.

- **Lorne Doerkson (Conservative).** Sourced background: MLA for Cariboo-Chilcotin since 2020, first elected as a B.C. Liberal; re-elected in 2024 as a B.C. Conservative (Elections BC results, 2024-10-19). BC Ballot gives the 2024 Conservative margin in the riding as 7,722 votes (bcballot.ca, 2026 candidate page). Carried forward from prior research, Elections BC's 2020 statement of votes shows him at 6,600 votes (51.25%) for the Liberals. The Globe and Mail (Sept. 26, 2026, carried forward) reports he took over as Conservative leader; Victoria News (Sept. 23, 2026) reports he is interim leader and says he would remain leader if elected premier.
  - *Controversy (campaign, 2026, allegation by a columnist):* Vaughn Palmer's Vancouver Sun column (Oct. 7, 2026, carried forward; paywalled in the copy read) says Doerkson told reporters he had made "no promises at all" on auto insurance, and Palmer argues he had made four. Palmer writes that Doerkson twice denied making commitments of any kind. Doerkson's response, as reported in that column, is the denial. This is the columnist's assessment, not a finding.
  - *Related party matter (not about Doerkson personally):* The Tyee (Oct. 8, 2026, carried forward) reports Doerkson fired the party's Victoria-Beacon Hill candidate after social media posts the BC NDP flagged as racist. CityNews (Oct. 14, 2026, carried forward) reports a Conservative campaign director under fire over social posts will stay on, Doerkson says.

- **Douglas Gook (BC Green).** Elections BC's candidate report and BC Green's candidate page list him for Cariboo-Chilcotin in 2026 (bcgreens.ca, 2026). Prior runs, as carried forward: the Caledonia Courier (Oct. 2024) reports he ran unsuccessfully four times as a Green candidate in North Cariboo, including a 2017 Nechako Lakes bid where he took about nine per cent. My Cariboo Now calls his 2020 bid his fourth run for the Greens in that riding. The two accounts do not reconcile the count of runs, and the show has not resolved it. The Elections BC 2020 statement of votes (carried forward) shows him at 707 votes (6.38%) in Cariboo North. CKPG Today (Sept. 13, 2024) announced him as the Green candidate for Nechako Lakes in 2024; his 2024 result is not established in the sources read. No controversy was established.

**FINDINGS — Prince George-North Cariboo (includes Quesnel)**

On the ballot: Denice Bardua (BC NDP), Sheldon Clare (Conservative), Randy Thompson (BC Green). The Quesnel Cariboo Observer (Oct. 7, 2026) reports the list was confirmed by Elections BC after nominations closed Oct. 3; CKPG Today (Oct. 3, 2026) lists the same three.

- **Denice Bardua (BC NDP).** CKPG Today (Sept. 24, 2024) reports she was announced as the NDP candidate in 2024. Her campaign site says she has been a Quesnel resident since 1997 and works in education (denicebardua.bcndp.ca). Her 2024 run: second place with 3,426 votes, 17.03%, behind independent Coralee Oakes (4,394 votes, 21.84%) and ahead of Conservative candidate Sheldon Clare's riding total... see note below (Elections BC, Statement of Votes, 43rd Provincial General Election, Oct. 19, 2024). The Quesnel Cariboo Observer (Oct. 7, 2026) gives the same 17.03%. No controversy was established.
  - Note: the Elections BC statement lists Clare first with 11,430 votes (56.82%); Bardua is second among the other candidates behind Oakes. Her 2024 run is the only earlier run established in the sources read.

- **Sheldon Clare (Conservative, incumbent).** Sourced background: won the riding for the B.C. Conservatives in 2024 (Elections BC results, 2024-10-19). Elections BC's 2024 statement of votes (Oct. 19, 2024) shows him at 11,430 votes, 56.82%. Quesnel Cariboo Observer (Oct. 7, 2026, carried forward) reports the same figure.
  - *Leadership bid (2026):* Times Colonist (Jan. 8, 2026, Canadian Press, carried forward) reports he said he was running for the B.C. Conservative leadership. CKPG Today (Jan. 20, 2026) reports he formally launched the bid. CFJC Today (Feb. 28, 2026, carried forward) reports he suspended it, citing a leadership application issue in which some signatures were not accepted; he said he "takes full responsibility."
  - *Election-finance penalty (finding):* Elections BC's enforcement notice (dated March 30, 2026) and its April 1, 2026 release, as reported by CKPG Today (Apr. 1, 2026) and the Quesnel Cariboo Observer (Apr. 3, 2026), say he was fined $1,500 for accepting anonymous contributions for the 2024 election that exceeded the limit by about $4,000. Elections BC said the investigation found no deliberate attempt to circumvent the law. The Prince George Citizen reported the same penalty. His response to the penalty was not found in the sources read.
  - *Allegation (Sept. 2026):* CKPG Today (Sept. 18, 2026, carried forward) reports that in a party group chat about municipal elections, Clare wrote "There's a good number that need hanging," responding to a post by a Parksville mayoral candidate. Clare's statement, as reported in the same coverage, says the remark was made in jest, was not meant as a threat, and he apologized to anyone who took offense. The Prince George Citizen headlined the apology as formal. The BC NDP criticized the remark on X (carried forward; full wording not read). This is an allegation with a response, not a finding.

- **Randy Thompson (BC Green).** CKPG Today (Oct. 20, 2026) reports this is his second run for public office, as the B.C. Green candidate in the riding, and that he is focusing on health care and forestry (ckpgtoday.ca, Oct. 20, 2026). His first run: the BC Greens' candidate page says he ran as the BC Green candidate in Prince George-North Cariboo in the 2024 provincial election, and that he served two years on the party's provincial council (bcgreens.ca, 2026). Elections BC's 2024 statement of votes shows him fourth with 866 votes, 4.31%. The Prince George Citizen (2026) gives 4.3%, fourth place. My Prince George Now's election-night count (848, 4.30%) is superseded by the official statement. No controversy was established.

Where the show has not established a record, in one sentence: the show has not yet established Askew's 2025 federal vote share or Gook's 2024 Nechako Lakes result.
